The Amazon logo is seen at one of its offices The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and a bipartisan group of 22 states has filed a lawsuit alleging Amazon secretly overcharged more than a million advertising customers by manipulating online auctions it uses to set ad prices. The FTC and states say in their lawsuit filed Monday that the alleged scheme has likely netted the company $20bn from advertising customers since 2019. "Amazon overrides and replaces the actual auction results with higher prices set by Amazon to increase its profits," says a complaint filed in the company's home state of Washington. In a statement to the BBC, Amazon "strongly disagrees" with the premise that it misled advertisers and called the suit "misguided." In addition to advertisers, the FTC, a US consumer watchdog, and the states say Amazon customers have also been harmed as extra costs are passed onto shoppers. "Consumers are suffering, have suffered, and will continue to suffer substantial injury as a result," the complaint states, prompting swift pushback from Amazon. "The FTC wants the public to believe this case is about higher prices for consumers. It is not," Amazon said in its statement. The company's shares fell following the announcement of the lawsuit, closing 2.5% lower on Monday. Many brands and sellers compete on Amazon to place Sponsored Product ads and Sponsored Brands ads when consumer search for products using keywords on Amazon's e-commerce platform. Those placements are then auctioned off to the highest bidder. The complaint accuses Amazon of secretly charging advertisers more in so-called "second price" auctions, whereby prospective advertisers expect to pay one cent more than the next highest bidder for each bid they win. But in practice, the complaint alleges, Amazon has charged its Sponsored Products advertisers their own winning bid close to 80% of the time. The lawsuit states that Amazon's methods were spurred because "it was unhappy about how much revenue its advertising auctions were generating".  Amazon responded by saying the FTC "fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate".  "Advertisers adjust bids based on real-world performance, not descriptions of auction mechanics," Amazon said in its statement. "Average winning bids fell 50% from 2019 to 2025 on Sponsored Products search ads, and roughly 92% of placed ads are not given to the highest bid," the company added. Amazon has tangled with the consumer watchdog in the past. Last year, it settled a case with the FTC that alleged that it enrolled millions of consumers in its Prime subscription offering without their consent, and knowingly made it difficult for consumers to cancel. Amazon settled the case for $2.5bn, including civil penalties and consumer refunds. Amazon agrees to pay $2.5bn over claims it tricked Prime customers Why does Amazon have no Western rivals? Some farmers say they're fed up, also pointing to the Iran war and tariffs. Matt Ubel, a farmer based in rural Wheaton, Kansas, says that high diesel and fertilizer prices driven by the war in Iran were already hurting his bottom line.  Now, he says he expects his profit margins will take another hit after President Donald Trump approved a temporary lift on tariffs for foreign inputs of 300,000 metric tons of beef to take effect in September.  "This wasn't about making cheaper groceries for the American people," Ubel told ABC News. "They need to invest in their farmers -- not import beef from other countries. They need to make farming sustainable here in the United States."  Ubel, the vice president of the Kansas Farmers Union who is also running for Pottawatomie County commissioner, cares for some 120 cattle. His frustrations reflect the ways Trump's trade policies could complicate GOP messaging on affordability just months out from the November midterms as Republicans fight to maintain control of Congress. Ubel said he voted for former President Barack Obama in 2012, but went for Trump in the last three presidential elections. Some districts in agriculturally dominant states with the largest volume of cattle sales are the most competitive this election cycle, U.S. Department of Agriculture data from 2022 shows. Those include Kansas and Nebraska, but also Iowa -- home to a highly contested gubernatorial race and a slate of congressional races -- and Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District, which could help determine control of Congress. The White House defended Trump's move, saying it's about both short-term and long-term needs. "The U.S. beef market is currently grappling with insufficient supply to meet consumer demand, and the President’s action is helping meet short-term beef needs while the Administration works with American ranchers to expand domestic production and grow the American cattle herd, which is currently at a multi-decade low," said Kush Desai, a spokesman for the White House.  The National Cattleman’s Beef Association, which represents America's cattle producers and beef industry, is pushing back on Trump’s plan for a law to allow farmers and ranchers to "PROCESS THEIR OWN FOOD," saying it's "weakening federal meat inspection & food safety standards isn’t the answer." Scott Thomsen, a fourth-generation Nebraska farmer, said he is calling it quits with the GOP.  "We have higher inflation, higher debt, a new war, and we're not America First when we're talking about importing beef," Thomsen said.  Last year, the three-time Trump voter said he was worried about a prolonged trade war but told ABC News he trusted in the Trump administration's plan to rebalance trade with China.  That was before the war in the Middle East spiked the cost of diesel fuel and fertilizer. And the president's new plan to import ground beef has rattled many ranchers. Renewed threats against Canada and "Economic D-Day" on Iran added further uncertainty to the future.  Thomsen said he is also angry with Nebraska's Republicans in Congress, who he said made "really soft" statements opposing the president's plan to import ground beef and did not "call out President Trump directly." "They've supported this war. They voted for this debt. They've voted for this inflation, so I think me and a lot of people are having a hard time voting for anybody who is in office right now and anybody who's representing us right now," Thomsen said. Several Nebraska Republicans have denounced Trump's move. Nebraska Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, who is running for reelection, wrote in a social media post that "flooding the market with lower quality beef compromises Nebraska farmers and ranchers." Nebraska Republican Sen. Deb Fischer, who is a cattle rancher herself, posted a similar message on social media, saying that Trump's beef plan "hurts our livestock industry and undermines the long-term solution: growing the U.S. cattle herd to meet demand." Thomsen's feelings -- and those of other young Republicans like him -- could keep otherwise supportive Trump voters from showing up for Republicans in a year when Democrats and many independents are energized to vote against the GOP.  Back in Kansas, where there is a competitive gubernatorial race, Ubel said he's split between Trump-endorsed Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson and Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher. Holscher blasted Trump for the administration's move to pause beef tariffs and Masterson for his silence, writing on social media that her Republican opponent is "nowhere to be found when Kansans need him."  For his part, Masterson broke with the president, according to a statement his campaign provided to ABC News. "Ty Masterson stands with Kansas ranchers. Everyone wants lower prices at the grocery store, and the way to get there is to help American ranchers rebuild the herd, not import foreign beef," Garrett Henson, a spokesperson for Masterson's campaign, told ABC News. "Ty shares the President's goal of lowering costs for families, and as governor he'll work with Kansas livestock producers, the best in the nation, to bring prices down: by cutting their costs, getting government out of their way, and growing the Kansas herd." The potential bruising effects of the U.S.-Canada trade war also concerns Ubel, who said there are "bigger issues at hand."  "I get where we're trying to come from with all these trade wars, but Canada has historically been a pretty good neighbor, so why do we want to keep ruffling that feather?" Ubel told ABC News.  During a radio interview with conservative host Glenn Beck last week, Trump called Canada one of "the worst countries" in the world to deal with and that they have taken "advantage" of the U.S. The country's trade war with China over soybeans already made Ubel pivot. He and his brother purchased their family farm in 2015, and they typically farm crops such as corn, soybeans, wheat and milo.  "But the last two years, with the trade war and everything going on, the soybean market wasn't there, and our opportunity was in corn," Ubel said.  In the northeastern rural town of Robinson, Kansas, Jack Geiger, a cattleman running as an independent for the state House of Representatives, also expressed disappointment with the decision to ease tariffs on beef imports. The timing of the administration's move bothered him, too, he said. "It's an attempt to do it earlier so that market does not get quote-unquote a head of steam going into the midterm elections," Geiger said. "The intervention last year happened in October. The intervention this year is happening in August."  Geiger, who also sits on the board of the Kansas Farmers Union, told ABC News that commodity producers had already been feeling the effects of inflation since 2022 -- and it isn't getting any easier. "The reality is we have an aging farm population," Geiger said. "We have decreased herd numbers, and we also have consumer demand for protein products that has been increasing dramatically." Kansas GOP incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall, a Trump ally up for reelection, criticized the president's move on beef import tariffs on social media. "Americans aren’t short on protein options like chicken or pork. What’s short is the signal to US ranchers to grow the herd back," Marshall wrote.  In a tele-town hall on Friday, the senator sought to assuage concerns, telling constituents that he would work to bring down the cost of fertilizer but defended the war in the Middle East, saying, "we cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon." Marshall said that he, too, is "frustrated" by Trump's decision on foreign beef imports but pointed to the national decline in U.S. cattle herd. And he maintained that the country's "cattle markets are really solid." "We just don't make enough hamburger in this country," Marshall said.   Ubel, however, said the administration's move was not about "cheaper hamburgers" but rather "market movement" to farmers' detriment.  And he said he is considering voting for Marshall's Democratic opponent, Rev. Adam Hamilton, a self-described moderate leading the largest United Methodist church in the country. Hamilton has flayed his Republican opponent for not holding public town halls -- an argument that resonates with Ubel. "If you're going to represent our state, come talk to me in person," Ubel said.  But the farmer -- who has railed against the two-party system -- said he is also unhappy with the Democrats.  "Both parties have lost touch with reality, and I think it's time that we start voting for people -- not the party," Ubel said.  He added: "We do have a say … and our vote counts." 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

Published         Aug 31, 2026      Contents On August 29, 2026, Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission’s Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, confirmed the first formal enforcement step under the EU AI Act: “As a first step in enforcing the AI Act, our AI Office has formally sent requests for information to a number of providers of general-purpose AI models based in different regions of the world. These requests concern model security, independent external evaluations, and the monitoring of models once they are available on the market.” Euractiv’s exclusive identifies the recipients as leading frontier labs, reportedly including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. The timing is the story: general-purpose AI obligations became enforceable on August 2, 2026, and Brussels used its new powers within four weeks. The viral framing - “Expect AI models to be unaccessible in the EU soon” - is a prediction, not a policy. Nothing announced blocks any model from the European market. What actually happened is narrower and, in its own way, more consequential: the Commission opened a formal supervisory file on the providers behind the models most people touch through an API, and it did so with an instrument that carries legal teeth. Under the Commission’s enforcement framework, replies that are incorrect, incomplete, or misleading can be fined up to 15 million euros or 3% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher, and ignoring an RFI triggers follow-up demands, then penalties. In serious cases the AI Office can require corrective measures or restrict a model’s public availability in the EU - that last power is where worries like the one in the post above come from, but using it requires findings that do not exist yet. Two separate RFIs went out, per Virkkunen’s announcement: Providers are legally required to respond, and the answers become part of a permanent supervisory record. The Commission has said it is “ready to take all necessary steps to ensure that companies comply with their obligations under the AI Act.” The RFIs do not come out of nowhere. July and August 2026 produced a string of frontier-model containment failures: the OpenAI agent swarm that reached root on Hugging Face production nodes, then retrospective reviews from Anthropic and Meta finding Claude and Muse Spark models breached external systems after a third-party evaluator’s misconfigured environments leaked real world access, and a UK AI Security Institute report of 19 documented unsanctioned actions against real systems during cyber evaluations. Brussels has confirmed parallel bilateral talks with OpenAI and Anthropic over the escape incidents - reportedly the first formal engagement by any major jurisdiction on models getting out of controlled test environments. Virkkunen opened her post with the same diagnosis: “AI models are becoming increasingly capable and gave rise to a number of incidents during the summer.” The contrast with Washington is stark. The US response to the same incidents is a finalized but unpublished evaluation framework built on voluntary cooperation. The EU’s version has fines, deadlines, and a paper trail. Read the enforcement targets carefully: the RFIs go to providers of general-purpose AI models - companies that place models on the European market. Nobody in Brussels is asking how you run a model on your own hardware, and the models and variants in the catalog that ship as open weights are, for now, largely on the receiving end of scrutiny only at their original publisher. The genuinely sharp question came from engineer Natan Katz in response to Virkkunen’s post: “If someone fine-tuned an HF model, you have no real information about the datasets.” Downstream fine-tunes of open models are exactly the gray zone a training-summary regime cannot reach - provenance dies at the first fork, and the forks are where most local runs live. The realistic read for the next few months: more information demands, publicized evaluation activity, and the first corrective actions aimed at specific providers. Whether that path ends anywhere near “unaccessible in the EU” is a question for whoever answers the requests badly. For the self-hosting side, the practical takeaway is unchanged by any of this: the model on your own disk has no terms of service and no jurisdiction, and the rig finder will point you at hardware that can run it. Samsung's book-style foldables have historically featured squarish (1:1) aspect ratios for their main displays, but the Galaxy Z Fold 8 changes that. It's a wider foldable with a 7.6-inch folding display that uses a 4:3 aspect ratio. As a result, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is better for widescreen video and mobile games, such as modern TV shows, movies, and game titles you're likely to play on an Android foldable. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 makes a handful of compromises to get there, so it's not for everyone. Luckily, the Android foldable market is ripe with options — and Apple is said to be gearing up to launch a wide "iPhone Ultra" foldable as well. For now, there are five Android phones I'd consider instead of the Galaxy Z Fold 8. Whether you're looking for great displays, long battery life, sharp cameras, or maximum durability, there's something for everyone here.  Why you can trust Android Central     Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.       Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 is fun to use, but it isn't the flagship foldable of 2026. That would be the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, which is a pricey pick at $2,100. This phone uses the same Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset and runs the same One UI 9 software. However, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra offers enough upgrades to be your top alternative to the Galaxy Z Fold 8. The nearly square folding display is better for multitasking, but it's also larger, with an 8-inch folding AMOLED screen. The cover screen is bigger, too, at 6.5 inches, and its aspect ratio makes the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra feel like a traditional smartphone. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is almost a millimeter thinner and is crazy light, weighing only 215 grams. Somehow, Samsung managed to cram a 5,000mAh silicon-carbon battery in this slim chassis — larger than the one in the regular Galaxy Z Fold 8. Plus, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra includes a triple-camera system on the rear, headlined by a 200MP primary shooter. The ultrawide camera is upgraded to a 50MP sensor this year, and the system is rounded out with a 10MP telephoto. All these spec bumps combine to make the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra a more well-rounded foldable than the Galaxy Z Fold 8, as long as you can live without the wide form factor.      If battery life is your main priority, there's no better choice than the Motorola Razr Fold. It runs on a 6,000mAh silicon-carbon battery that charges at blazing 80W wired charging speeds and 50W wireless charging, as long as you use a proprietary charger. The Razr Fold has the largest foldable battery you'll find in the U.S., and it's still only 9.89mm thick. It is on the heavier side, but Motorola makes up for that with stylish vegan leather materials and a premium look. The Razr Fold uses an 8.1-inch folding display that's larger than every other foldable on this list. It's also really bright at up to 6,200 nits. What's interesting is that the Razr Fold's 6.6-inch cover screen has a 165Hz refresh rate, making it more responsive than the Galaxy Z Fold 8. Another perk of Motorola's first book-style foldable is its camera system, which we even compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8 series. Every rear camera lens, from the primary shooter to the ultrawide and telephoto, uses a 50MP sensor. This gives you plenty of versatility, whereas the Galaxy Z Fold 8's ultrawide camera is low-resolution and lacks a telephoto. The Razr Fold's base Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 chip might give you pause, but it shouldn't. Even without an "Elite" processor, the Razr Fold performs as it should.      Samsung is trying to start a new foldable trend with the Galaxy Z Fold 8. Apple might introduce a wide foldable of its own with the iPhone Ultra, but until then, there's only one widescreen alternative to the Galaxy Z Fold 8: the original Google Pixel Fold. Released in 2023, the Pixel Fold has a 7.6-inch folding display with a wide 6:5 aspect ratio that feels similar to the Galaxy Z Fold 8. If you're set on trying a widescreen foldable, the Pixel Fold is the only real alternative. The Tensor G2 chipset is showing its age, but the Pixel Fold's other core specs still hold up in 2026. You get a 4,821mAh battery, a triple-camera system, and a 5.8-inch cover screen. The phone is still fully supported with Android updates. You can run Android 17 on it today, and it's guaranteed to get at least Android 18. What makes the Pixel Fold truly appealing is the price. If you can find it in new or refurbished condition, it'll be around $500 or less. On the secondhand market, it's not hard to find a Pixel Fold for $300 or less. That's a steal for a foldable, even one that's a few years old. It might be worth your while to track down an original Pixel Fold to get a Galaxy Z Fold 8 competitor with a wide-folding display at a low price.      Part of the appeal of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is its compact form factor when closed. Though it's a little wide, the Galaxy Z Fold 8's 5.5-inch cover screen is much more compact than modern Android phones. If you're intrigued by the smaller footprint, the Galaxy Z Flip 8 might be worth a look. As a flip phone, it's certainly a different experience than the Galaxy Z Fold 8, but it comes with practical benefits of its own. The Galaxy Z Flip 8 is lighter than the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and measures only 85.7 tall when shut, making it disappear in your pocket. Plus, it has the same Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy chipset, meaning you can expect similar performance across the two phones. Samsung kept the same 4,300mAh battery in the Galaxy Z Flip 8, but it charges fairly fast at 25W via cable. That gets you about 55% of the battery in exchange for a 30-minute charge. The phone has a 6.9-inch display when unfolded, putting it in the Galaxy S26 Plus and Galaxy S26 Ultra territory. The 4.1-inch cover screen is usable, and the software is slowly getting better. At $1,200, the Galaxy Z Flip 8 is about $700 cheaper than the Galaxy Z Fold 8. It might not be exactly what you had in mind when you started searching for a new foldable, but flip phones are fun, functional, and more affordable.      Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold does two things better than any other foldable sold in the U.S.: durability and wireless charging. It's still the only foldable to be completely dustproof thanks to IP68 certification, meaning you don't have to worry about dust or sand working their way into your folding display assembly or hinge and causing trouble. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold also has Qi2 magnets inside. This allows you to connect the Pixel 11 Pro Fold to Qi2, MagSafe, or Pixelsnap chargers and accessories without needing a third-party case. This time, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold isn't overtly thick because of its internal magnets. The foldable measures 10.1mm thick, which is respectable. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is thinner, but doesn't have internal magnets. Google has a few more tricks up its sleeve, like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold's HiLight feature, a colorful LED on the back flash that glows when you receive a call from a favorite contact or start chatting with Gemini. It's a bit gimmicky, but it makes the Pixel 11 Pro Fold unique. This is one of many Pixel-exclusive features on the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, such as Magic Capture and Camera Looks. If you value IP68 and Qi2 as foldable features, you should choose the latest Google foldable over the Galaxy Z Fold 8. If none of these foldables catch your eye, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 may indeed be the best option for your needs. Otherwise, consider traditional flagships, like the Google Pixel 11 Pro XL and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. While they don't have the large folding displays of the other phones on this list, these models are just as capable and cost hundreds of dollars less. For years, the Raspberry Pi Zero lineup has been the go-to answer for the cheapest little computer you can drop into a project. At $15, it made sense for everything from a Pi-hole ad blocker to a homemade dashcam. But that math is now falling apart. Search for one today, and you'll find listings anywhere from $40 to $90, with a lot of sellers landing right around $60. It's not that Raspberry Pi suddenly repriced the board out of spite. It's a mix of scarcity, resale markups, and a wider memory crunch that's rattled the entire single-board computer market. Smaller board, same smart home. Raspberry Pi has been upfront that the increases sweeping its 2GB-and-up lineup come from surging DRAM and flash memory costs, and the company explicitly said it didn't expect changes to the Zero lineup because it still has a stockpile of the older LPDDR2 memory the Zero 2 W relies on. In theory, that should've kept the $15 price tag intact. In practice, official stock has been thin enough that resellers and marketplace listings have filled the gap at inflated prices, and that's the number most people are actually seeing when they go shopping. So you're not imagining things: the board is technically still $15 somewhere, but good luck finding it there. If you just want something that slots into the same physical footprint and does roughly the same job, the Orange Pi Zero 3 is the obvious first stop. It runs an Allwinner H618 quad-core chip, comes with 4GB of RAM, and ships with gigabit Ethernet and Wi-Fi 5, all for around $25 to $40 depending on where you buy it and whether you're importing directly. That's a genuine spec upgrade over the Zero 2 W's 512MB of RAM and single wireless band, and it's still cheaper than most inflated Zero listings. The Orange Pi Zero 2W is another solid option in the same price range, with similar wireless capability and a slightly different memory ceiling. The catch with Orange Pi boards, however, is the software polish. Armbian and community images work fine for headless server tasks like Pi-hole, Home Assistant add-ons, or a lightweight file sharing server, but don't expect the same first-boot smoothness Raspberry Pi OS delivers. Orange Pi Zero 3 is a compact, low-cost single-board computer powered by the Allwinner H618 processor, offering Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Gigabit Ethernet, and enough performance for home servers, networking projects, and lightweight Linux workloads. If your project requires GPIO pins for sensors, motors, or HATs, the Banana Pi BPI-M2 Zero is also worth a look. It physically mirrors the Zero's layout and has been used as a drop-in replacement in maker circles for years, generally landing between $18 and $25. It won't match the newer Allwinner chips on raw performance, but for basic automation and sensor logging, it does the job without asking you to redesign your enclosure or rewire your breakout board. Banana Pi BPI-M5 is a powerful single-board computer built around the Amlogic S905X3 processor, featuring 4GB RAM, Gigabit Ethernet, eMMC storage support, and enough performance for home servers, containers, and media applications. Not every Zero replacement needs to be small. If size isn't a constraint, and your project needs faster storage, more RAM, or genuine multitasking, the Le Potato is a better long-term bet than chasing another Zero-sized board. It costs around $35, uses an Amlogic S905X chip with real 64-bit cores, and keeps GPIO pin compatibility with a lot of existing Pi accessories. It's larger than a Zero, so it's not for tight enclosures, but for home server duty or a retro gaming box, it punches well above its price. Libre Computer Le Potato is a budget-friendly single-board computer based on the Amlogic S905X processor, offering Raspberry Pi-compatible GPIO, 4K video output, and solid Linux support for media centers, home servers, and DIY projects. Once you start compartmentalizing projects, you'll realize that you don't actually need Linux, a desktop environment, or even a filesystem for a lot of projects. If you're just reading a sensor, flipping a relay, or running a simple automation over Wi-Fi, an ESP32 development board handles it for well under $15 and sips a fraction of the power. Pair it with ESPHome and Home Assistant, and you get a purpose-built device that boots instantly and never needs an SD card. It's not a Pi replacement in the general sense, but for a lot of projects, it might just be the smarter buy. ESP32 is a low-cost microcontroller with built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, widely used for IoT projects and DIY electronics. There's no single board that replaces the Raspberry Pi Zero in every scenario, and that's fine. Match the replacement to the job: Orange Pi Zero 3 for general-purpose headless computing, Banana Pi M2 Zero if you need the exact form factor, Le Potato when you've outgrown zero-sized boards, and an ESP32 when Linux is overkill. Put your new, ultra-powerful Raspberry Pi 5 to good use. Checking current pricing before you buy is worth the extra five minutes, since availability on all these shifts week to week. Regardless, it's a great time for single-board computers, and you're not going to have a shortage of alternatives. All you need is the right board for the job. We want to hear from you. A weekend flare-up between the United States and Iran has pushed crude oil sharply higher, and the old gasoline-price trade in electric-vehicle names is getting another look this morning. The question in the title deserves a plain answer, and the direct one is that the mechanism is plausible while no company-specific catalyst has been confirmed for Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA | TSLA Price Prediction) today. The framing contrast matters here. Tesla stock is up 4% to $364.30 while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is down 0.6% to $764.93, so the move is specific to the stock rather than a rising broad market lifting everything. Zoom out and the day looks more isolated. Tesla stock was down 22% year to date through Friday’s close, so a single strong session is sitting inside a badly negative year for the name. WTI crude oil is at $86.06 per barrel, up 3% over the past 24 hours, and the driver is geopolitical. The United States and Iran resumed military strikes over the weekend, and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains constrained. That’s the risk premium moving energy this morning, and it’s what has revived a familiar debate about electric-vehicle demand. The thesis itself is straightforward. Higher gasoline prices improve the running-cost case for an electric vehicle against a comparable gasoline model, which can support EV demand at the margin. Pump prices are already stretched, with the national average price of regular gas at $4.08 per gallon, up 2.1% from a month ago, above the $4 level that historically registers with household budgets. This same argument was examined by 24/7 Wall St. during an earlier phase of the Iran conflict in April, and it hasn’t consistently held. Published skepticism earlier in 2026 argued that Tesla stock had stopped responding to oil-price spikes, and management commentary supports that reading. On Tesla’s July 22 second-quarter call, executives attributed vehicle demand to Full Self-Driving adoption and product appeal rather than fuel-price economics. Tesla CEO Elon Musk pointed to FSD as “a significant demand driver,” and finance chief Vaibhav Taneja stated, “One of the key factors for vehicle demand has been FSD.” So the Tesla-to-crude link is a mechanism rather than a proven cause, and history says the connection can fade as quickly as the risk premium does. If the gasoline logic were holding cleanly, the same read should extend to Rivian Automotive (NASDAQ:RIVN) and Lucid Group (NASDAQ:LCID) as the other pure electric-vehicle names in the group. Rivian and Lucid carry different fundamentals from Tesla, yet they occupy the same corner of the market the thesis would lift. That doesn’t mean the pass-through works evenly across Rivian, Lucid, and Tesla, and past episodes suggest it often doesn’t. Elevated fuel costs are at least registering with corporate management teams this week. Affirm Holdings (NASDAQ:AFRM) CEO Max Levchin, discussing his company’s results on Thursday, August 27, flagged rising gasoline prices as a pressure on consumers. Consumer sentiment supports the broader budget-pressure read, with the University of Michigan index at 55.2, still below the level the source classifies as recessionary. Position sizing deserves emphasis on a day like this. A Tesla rally built on a geopolitical risk premium in crude rather than on anything Tesla itself announced can reverse as fast as that premium does, so exposure taken on this session in Tesla stock carries headline risk in both directions. Shareholders adding to their Tesla positions on the strength should size those adds to the volatility of the underlying story, not to the size of the intraday move. The answer to the title question is a hedged yes. The mechanism is back on the table for Tesla, the setup rhymes with the April episode, and today’s action is behaving as if the trade might work again. Whether it holds beyond a headline-driven session in Tesla stock is a separate question, and one the last few episodes have answered with more nuance than conviction. In the group chat with my friends from high school, there's no more polarizing topic than baseball. We're divided pretty evenly between loyal diehards, and those who see baseball fading in relevance — a sport where only three or four teams are trying to win the World Series, and everyone else is just developing players to eventually trade to them. If you can't tell, I fit squarely into the latter camp. I can't watch a game without getting bored within five minutes. The gameplay is just too slow. So you can imagine my joy when I came across a research note from financial analytics firm S3 Partners that said short sellers are increasingly betting on a Major League Baseball lockout starting in December. The proxy S3 used was short interest in class C shares for the Atlanta Braves — the only publicly traded MLB club. The chart below shows that short interest as a percentage of equity float has surged since late May. The inflection point came on May 28, when MLB owners proposed a salary cap, which was a nonstarter for the players union and ratcheted up tension ahead of upcoming labor negotiations. (h/t Bloomberg for flagging that date.) Short-sellers have since piled into bets against Braves shares, which could suffer if a prolonged lockout hits next season. "Every week without a deal between December and spring training is the shorts' friend," the S3 research team wrote. To get into specifics, S3 found that there's been a record-setting 142% rise in total Braves shares shorted since the start of 2026. That includes a 14% increase in the last 30 days. It's also worth noting that Braves shares are sitting near record highs. The stock has benefited from soaring sports-franchise valuations, particularly following the record $12.5 billion sale of the LA Lakers. It's common for stocks at highs to attract short interest from investors looking to hedge. Still, the timing of the move makes the MLB labor standoff hard to ignore. Andrew Bailey put the assessment to G20 finance ministers in writing, alongside warnings about AI valuations and leverage. Andrew Bailey, the Governor of the Bank of England The chair of the Financial Stability Board has told G20 finance ministers that what artificial intelligence does to cyber risk is now the most immediate threat to the global financial system. Andrew Bailey set out the assessment in a letter ahead of this week’s meetings, Reuters reported on Monday. His argument is more about economics, as AI can change the speed, the scale and the cost of an attack, which is a different proposition from attackers simply having better tools. Bailey chairs the FSB alongside his day job as governor of the Bank of England, and the board exists to spot risks that cross borders and sectors before they become crises. Placing cyber above every other item on its list is not a routine move. The letter cited the incident in July when an OpenAI agent escaped its testing environment and hacked Hugging Face, which remains the clearest public example of a model doing unsupervised damage. The IMF reached a similar conclusion earlier this year, warning that AI is already fuelling cyberattacks against financial institutions. Two multilateral bodies arriving independently at the same ranking is the part supervisors tend to notice. Moreover, Bailey warned that many countries have no system for managing how advanced AI models get deployed inside their financial sectors. That is a gap in governance rather than in technology, and it is the kind of gap the FSB was built to name. A second concern runs alongside the first. The financial sector now depends on a handful of technology providers, and that concentration is itself a risk to confidence, because a failure at one supplier propagates through institutions that have no alternative to switch to. The board has been circling this for months. Bailey asked Anthropic to brief the FSB on what its Mythos model had been finding in May, after the system turned up thousands of high-severity vulnerabilities in widely used software. A briefing is a request for information, whereas a letter to G20 ministers naming a top concern is a regulator putting a position on the record before anyone asks. The cyber warning did not arrive alone. Bailey flagged stretched valuations in AI assets, frailties in government debt markets, and rising leverage in equity markets, a combination that describes an economy borrowing heavily against expectations of the same technology. The US Treasury has already intervened to cap bond yields that had reached multi-decade highs, which is the sort of action that tends to precede a broader conversation about market plumbing. Central bankers have been converging on this territory for a while. Christine Lagarde has argued that AI could trigger financial crises and called for governance modelled on Cold War non-proliferation, which is a considerably more dramatic framing than Bailey’s. Agentic systems are what turns this from a forecast into a supervisory problem. A model that can plan, act and persist across systems does not need a human operator at each step, which removes the labour cost that has always limited how many targets an attacker can work at once. The FSB has no power to compel anyone. It sets standards, publishes assessments and relies on national regulators to act, which means the practical effect of this letter depends entirely on what finance ministries choose to do with it. For European banks the relevant deadlines are already fixed. The Cyber Resilience Act took effect in September with vulnerability reporting windows measured in hours, and DORA has been governing operational resilience in financial services since 2025. Bailey’s letter arrived before the G20 sessions rather than after them, which is the point of it. Whether the ministers reading it agree that this belongs at the top of the list is the thing worth watching this week. SB Energy has handed OpenAI warrants now worth about $5.5bn, and it did so to keep OpenAI as a tenant. The Wall Street Journal reported the arrangement on Monday. The direction matters and is easy to get backwards. SB Energy, the SoftBank-owned power and data centre developer, is the issuer, and OpenAI is the recipient, which makes this a landlord paying its anchor tenant rather than a customer taking a stake. The instruments were granted in January and valued then at $3.6bn. By the end of June, they were worth $5.5bn, an increase of roughly $1.9bn driven by the rising value of the underlying equity rather than by anything OpenAI did. What they buy is a signature on a very long lease. OpenAI has committed to 20 years at SB Energy’s planned campus in southern Ohio, a ten-gigawatt site announced in mid-August with first operations targeted for 2028. OpenAI and SoftBank each put $500m into SB Energy, paired with a lease on a 1.2-gigawatt facility in Texas, and the warrants were awarded in the same period. Ten gigawatts is a figure worth pausing on. It is roughly the electrical demand of a mid-sized European country, committed to a single campus by a company that did not exist in its current form five years ago. SB Energy is also preparing to go public, targeting between $5bn and $7bn in proceeds. OpenAI is expected to hold a single-digit percentage stake after that listing, which turns a tenant into a shareholder at exactly the moment public investors are asked to value the company. Nvidia is in the same structure from a third direction. It has been weighing an investment of about $3bn in SB Energy tied to the Ohio project, according to The Information. Line those up, and the arrangement is circular by design. The chip supplier, the power developer, the model company and the parent that owns two of the four all hold financial positions in the same buildout, and each one’s valuation depends partly on the others continuing to commit. SoftBank has now committed more than $64bn across OpenAI equity, the joint SB Energy investments and Stargate. The stated logic is to own the model layer through OpenAI and the physical layer through SB Energy, which requires both to keep working. This is not the only place the pattern shows up. Nvidia has been in talks to guarantee $250bn of OpenAI data centre debt, also in Ohio, and lenders have grown noticeably more careful about the sector. The financing has been getting harder rather than easier. Oracle’s $16.3bn data centre package needed PIMCO to anchor $10bn after US banks stepped back, which is not what a comfortable market looks like. SoftBank has been raising against the same expectations. It signed a $40bn bridge facility in March to fund its OpenAI commitments, and has spent the months since looking for something permanent to replace it. Warrants are a useful instrument in that environment because they cost nothing today. SB Energy pays only if its own equity appreciates, and the dilution lands on whoever buys into the IPO rather than on the balance sheet now. There is also a question of who bears the risk if demand disappoints. A twenty-year lease is a liability on OpenAI’s side and an asset on SB Energy’s, and the warrants make OpenAI a beneficiary of the value its own signature creates. Neither OpenAI nor SB Energy has commented publicly on the terms, and the reporting rests on unnamed sources. What is on the record is the shape of the commitment: twenty years, ten gigawatts, and a set of instruments that have already appreciated by more than half before the site has broken ground. Tisch identified the first victim as a 68-year-old man who had just exited the subway and was waiting to cross the street alongside his wife. Police said Cisneros stabbed him in the right side of his abdomen. He was taken to Bellevue Hospital and is in stable condition, she said. Tisch said the second victim was a 32-year-old woman who was also stabbed in the abdomen and later pronounced dead at Bellevue. The NYPD commissioner said both attacks appeared to be random and unprovoked. Cisneros then continued north on Seventh Avenue, according to police. Officers encountered her between West 42nd and West 43rd streets while she was still armed with both knives. Tisch said officers “engaged the woman in dialogue for four minutes and gave her numerous commands to drop the knives, which she refused.” During the encounter, Tisch said Cisneros told officers, “I’m not dropping anything. Tisch said multiple officers deployed Tasers, but they were ineffective and Cisneros continued advancing with the knives. Two officers then fired their guns, striking her, authorities said. Both knives were recovered at the scene, according to police. Cisneros had no arrest history with the NYPD but had a "documented mental health history" with the department involving incidents in 2018 and 2019, Tisch said. Police did not provide additional details about those incidents. “This was an extraordinarily dangerous situation unfolding in the heart of Times Square, the crossroads of the world,” Tisch said. Florida is so much more than theme parks and sandy beaches — it's a place I've fallen in love with over the last 25 years for its gorgeous views, amazing weather, and the excitement of always finding something new to explore. As someone who has lived in Orlando for decades, I've traveled Florida from coast to coast and have learned of lots of hidden gems along the way. Here are seven places in Florida no tourist should miss. If you love history, St. Augustine, located on the northeast coast of Florida, is a dream destination. Known as the oldest continuously-settled city in the US, its brick streets and Spanish colonial architecture transport you back in time. Start with a tour of the Castillo de San Marcos, a centuries-old fort overlooking the Matanzas River. Then, wander through the shops and restaurants on St. George Street. Sanibel and Captiva Islands on Florida's Gulf Coast are the perfect destinations for a slower-paced getaway. Famous for their beautiful beaches and seashells, these islands are great for cycling and kayaking. I also suggest visiting the J.N. "Ding" Darling National Wildlife Refuge on Sanibel Island to spot manatees and colorful birds. These islands offer a laid-back vibe with incredible sunsets and some of the freshest seafood you'll ever taste. Stunning beaches, incredible nightlife, and a mix of art and culture make Miami a must-visit destination. I recommend exploring the colorful murals of Wynwood Walls, diving into Cuban culture in Little Havana, and strolling through the Art Deco buildings of South Beach. He added that other up-and-coming golf brands are waiting to take Good Good's place. The diversified business that had made Good Good a creator success story — and helped it raise $45 million last year — also exposed it to outside partners who didn't have the appetite to weather bad news. There could be other shoes still to drop, said Chris Erwin, founder of RockWater, an M&A and strategy advisory firm for the creator economy. For example, Good Good has a partnership with Dude Perfect, aimed at gaining a foothold with younger viewers, that could be at risk. Still, Erwin and others said all isn't lost for the brand. Good Good has a war chest, more than 2 million subscribers, and — ironically — a fresh wave of attention after the scandal. It also has a new president, who could help steady the ship. The channel could double down on its core audience with paid subscriptions, direct-sold products, and live events while it recovers. "It's a moment to show who they are," Erwin said. Action-AdventureCapcomOnimusha: Way of the SwordOpen world  Onimusha is a particularly challenging franchise for Capcom to revive, as it exists somewhat out of time. Itâs built on top of the design foundations of Resident Evil, and its development directly inspired Devil May Cry; it is, in a sense, the missing link between what Capcomâs 3D action games were and what they would become. This left the series in a weird spot after the runaway success of Devil May Cry, attempting to find some way to hold on to its identity, its entries growing longer and less focused even as the genre moved in a very different direction, until valiantly giving up the fight in 2006.Â  And what was that identity? Its first pillar was one of pure cinematic ambition. Onimusha games cast real, star actors in grand, digital Jidaigeki: Takeshi Kaneshiro was the seriesâ samurai hero Samanosuke, Jean Reno was a time-travelling French policeman. Way of the Sword, the seriesâ first entry in 20 years, certainly continues this need to borrow star power in a show of cinematic legitimacy, with the somewhat questionable decision to âcastâ long-dead legend of the screen Toshiro Mifune as the famous warrior-poet Miyamoto Musashi, echoing his role in Hiroshi Inagakiâs Samurai trilogy.Â  Its second pillar was its unique evolution of Resident Evilâs design language, combining spatial exploration and resource management with a strong melee combat system. In its simplest form, Onimusha asked the question, âHow can we build the experience of Knife-Only Runs into their own holistic game?â The result was still a game about routing, herding and spacing, but one that inverted the way that Resident Evilâs resource management and combat were linked. Here, instead of collecting ammunition that could be spent to dispatch enemies, attacking was free, but enemies dropped souls used for upgrades and ammunition. With every enemy, a choice was presented: you could use the traditional tank controls to avoid their attacks and use your own to earn a normal amount of souls, or hold your ground and time your attack perfectly for a deadly counter that reaped a much greater reward. This mechanic, the Issen, became the central core of Onimushaâs identity. If an Onimusha game had to have one thing, it had to have the Issen. Onimusha: Way of the Sword has the Issen. But it does not contain any of Onimushaâs other design fundamentals. Instead of a coherent interconnected space you explore throughout the game, there is an open world with side missions and collectables. Instead of deliberate, restricted movement and spacing, there is a heavy lock-on with strong magnetism and tracking on both Musashiâs attacks and those of his enemies. Instead of a focused resource system that emphasizes decision making in combat, thereâs a sprawling amount of currencies feeding into several overlapping, incremental upgrade systems. This is Capcomâs answer for how to bring back Onimusha: to strip it entirely to its perceived core and to replace everything else with something that looks superficially similar, if you squint. The result is a game at war with itself, where each decision collides with every other in a series of unsatisfying compromises. Let us focus first on where Onimusha: Way of the Sword also chooses to focus: combat. Onimushaâs original design focused on that risk/reward choice between avoiding being hit and standing your ground. Turning was restricted and movement was deliberate. Avoiding attacks meant carefully considering where you were standing, and the best strategy was to simply not be in the place where the enemy attacked in the first place. Standing your ground meant risking eating that hit, but opened up access to your Issen counter. This was an intuitive and engaging system, but it had one unignorable structural weakness: The Issen is a binary mechanic. Unlike movement, which due to variances in your inputs and enemy behavior, has near-infinite ways to be performed, ranging from embarrassing to masterful, the Issen is either performed correctly or it isnât. Once you have learned the Issen timings on every enemy, the risk/reward dynamic that makes each encounter so engaging loses its risk. This was not a great concern in the original game, being only four hours long, but as the games got longer and the audienceâs experience with the series grew, different Issen variations were introduced in order to add more decision-making into combat, with varying levels of success. Way of the Sword continues this trend and takes it to an extreme, while throwing the baby out with the bathwater. First, movement has been so downplayed as to be taken out of the equation almost entirely. Musashi has a generous slide towards enemies when he attacks, and enemies lunge towards you with heavy tracking. When in a one v oneâwhich the majority of the gameâs boss fights and setpiece encounters areâyou only have to worry about not standing too close to a wall and sending the camera off its axis completely. Capcom knows the Issen alone is not enough, so in order to compensate for this new approach to movement, your defensive toolkit has been expanded to a suite of five (count âem) different timing-based reaction mechanics. There is the Issen, the parry, the reflex dodge, the deflect, and the blade barrage. Way of the Swordâs combat design is primarily around throwing different attacks at you which require different responses and different timings, and which give different advantages. It will be compared a lot to Sekiro, and this comparison is not inaccurate, but I find a better touchstone for both its strengths and weaknesses is Punch-Out!! Fighting a boss in Way of the Sword is very similar to bouts in Punch-Out!! Both require you to respond to animations with the correct (and correctly timed) input. Both have varying levels of punishment and strictness for your execution of these challenges within each fight. The satisfaction comes from slowly learning the patterns and internalizing the correct responses, until you reach the level of mastery where your opponent is unable to land a single strike no matter what they do. Within its boss fights, Way of the Sword is capable of reaching these peaks. These duels can, as the game progresses, get brutally difficult, and as you reach new ones, they may consistently cause you to ask yourself how winning such a thing is even possible. But they can all be overcome with observance, perseverance, and keeping your cool.Â  No single attack is that hard, no mandatory timing window so tight that it feels impossible. Instead, Way of the Sword asks for consistency. Hang in there. Donât give up. Youâve parried that attack before. And with Capcomâs sound and effects team, the impact of these hits when you finally perform them correctly is music to the ears. These boss fights are excellent, and overcoming them is the gameâs true appeal. Despite everything else, the quality of this specific experience is what will make the whole thing worth it, and guarantees this game a passionate audience. You might read the many complaints in this review, and still think youâll be one of those passionate players, and to you I say godspeed and fight true: these boss fights are absolutely the new vision of Onimusha at its best. But I make this comparison mostly because it highlights Onimushaâs fatal flaw far easier than anything else I could say: Punch-Out!! is not 25 hours long and you donât fight a Soda Popinski miniboss seven times. Outside the context of boss fights, Way of the Swordâs combat system collapses like a house of cards. To account for the strength of your defensive options, boss movesets are oppressive and intense, challenging you to find gaps to heal, even punishing you for disengaging to camp with enemies’ fast-recharging stamina. None of this is true in mob fights. Here, your defensive options must be accounted for but in the other direction. Musashiâs moveset focuses on single-target parries, so enemies patiently take turns to attack in order to ensure your core moveset remains viable. Issens in the original had a hitbox, so herding enemies to take out multiple with a single counter was a valid and effective strategy. Here, Issens are locked animations, and can only be chained with another timed button press or by depleting enemy stamina. These fundamental flaws are never addressed, instead merely papered over as the game makes basic enemies tankier, or adds armor which functions exclusively as a âpress the armor-breaking buttonâ quick time event. For 95 percent of the game, youâll be approaching mobs of enemies not as coherent groups whose composition meaningfully changes the encounter, but as individuals you rigidly defeat in a pre-determined fashion, one by one. You will be bored of an enemy type after their third appearance. You will be fighting that enemy for tens of hours. And you will question all the choices that led you here when the game starts regularly recycling minibosses. This would be bad if Way of the Sword was just a linear action game, but it is not. It is an open-world game, and that means it doesnât just have encounters and levels, it has Content. It means that, between main missions, you may spend your time running through repeated areas, doing the same parries on the same enemies for even more hours. It means running around the map, collecting 2 Iron and 1 Whetstone to increase sword damage by 2 percent. It means navigating by markers and breadcrumb trails and occasionally pressing your detective-vision button to find a hidden chest in that dead end. The choice to make Way of the Sword an open-world game is by far the single choice that most poisons the dish. It brings no benefits, and is completely at odds with everything else about the gameâs design. Itâs simply not fun to fight an enemy again after youâve already passed the test of how to fight that enemy. Upgrade materials are stretched so thin that you either have to spend literal hours engaged in mind-numbingly tedious resource collection to meaningfully reap the benefits, or to accept being underpowered for the bulk of the game. Itâs a design decision that feels driven by pure obligation, because releasing a game of this size and scope without repeatable morsels of content spread throughout is simply unthinkable at seventy dollars. The tragedy, of course, is that Onimusha always had repeatable content: it was called replaying the game. Which brings us full circle, at last, to the story. In an outcome most faithful to the original, this new Onimusha is a lavishly produced game with grand cinematic ambitions all done in the service of a generic, disappointing story. This would be fine if the rest of the game was both well-paced and constantly engaging, like it was in 2001. But Way of the Sword is neither, and so its narrative failings are even more pronounced. This is emphasized by the choice to use Mifuneâs young face, as you watch a digital replica of one of historyâs greatest actors send you to sleep with stock shonen tropes. If you have ever wanted Toshiro Mifune to say âMy friends are my power!â while going Super Saiyan, this game is for you, though that sentence definitely makes this sound more appealing than it is. The generic sensibilities of the writing contrast poorly with the overly grey visuals and photoscanned actors, and it all leads to a story that isnât fun enough to embrace how dumb it is, but isnât good enough to get away with how dour it is.Â  The game is filled to bursting with famous historical figures, but is bafflingly uninterested in using them for anything fun. Way of the Sword is set in Kyoto in the early days of the Tokugawa Shogunate, and you visit the Imperial Palace, but no one ever explains what either of those things are at this very interesting point in history. It feels like such a missed opportunity. The original Onimusha games did not have particularly great stories either, but they did have fun getting up to some true Metal Gear-type nonsense with how they tied their Oni alt-history to specific battles and events in the Sengoku era. Way of the Sword is a heartbreakingly confused and compromised game. There is an excellent core in there, even if that core has very little to do with anything previously called Onimusha. But that core of quality boss encounters only takes up anywhere from ten to thirty percent of its playtime, depending on how much time you spend either dying over and over or doing optional content in the open world. The remaining bulk of the game flits between, in the best case, a poor fit for its core mechanical design, and in the worst case, an active waste of everyoneâs time. It is not badly made or incompetent, but torn apart by concessions to market expectations and the scope obligations of games produced at this budget. Radar > Topics > Zero to Agent in 30 Minutes A multi-agent workflow that turns scattered financial news into analyst briefings   By Michelle Smith August 31, 2026 • 3 minute read In this episode of Zero to Agent in 30 Minutes, Jayeeta Putatunda, forward deployed AI engineering lead at Turing, builds a multi-agent workflow that turns a daily flood of financial headlines into a structured analyst briefing. Financial analysts already have deep internal research, coverage assignments, and market views, but keeping that context current as new information arrives every day and surfacing which of it actually deserves an analyst’s attention is a harder problem. Jayeeta built the entire stack on open source models so newcomers can run it without an API key, and she recommends starting with a smaller model before scaling up. The takeaway extends well beyond finance. Building single-purpose agents rather than one large agent that handles every task means a failure at one stage doesn’t force a restart of the whole pipeline, and each agent’s output stays easier to trace and debug. I was talking to a founder who builds software for banks, and we drifted onto a theme I have not been able to let go of since: AI is aiding disintermediation and quietly removing vendor lock-in. If you think of old-school tech lock-in, perhaps the best example you can think of is banks and mainframes. The code is decades old, the vendor knows everything about it, and nobody on the inside wants to touch a migration. This is the founder’s business. Between the contract lengths and the termination fees, he told me, “It’s very, very sticky, and it’s very, very hard to move away.” That stickiness has been the business model for a big chunk of enterprise software. I think it is about to stop working, and the way I would frame it is as an opportunity for small businesses, in two different directions. Software vendors in particular assumed that if they served a piece of your technical infrastructure, they would be tricky to get rid of. And for most of the last few years, this has been true. If you provided someone with their core banking infrastructure, or the CRM system they use to manage their sales and customers and so on, well, it was risky to migrate away from you. Companies like Salesforce have managed to latch onto a huge part of the digital economy simply by being the vendor of choice and making it very difficult, risky and cumbersome to leave. Banking shows how extreme this gets. Reuters counted 220 billion lines of COBOL still in production, a 1959 language propping up 43% of banking systems. Leaving one of the big core providers, the founder told me, has meant “dedicated teams to work through migrations over the course of 18 to 24+ months in order to move from one provider to the other.” But AI risks changing all of this, for a few reasons. The technical barriers are lower, and the incremental grunt work needed to migrate is less of an issue. AI can now write COBOL, and IBM sells a code assistant whose main pitch is translating mainframe COBOL into Java. Meanwhile, as a consumer, I can export all of my data from Google, from Meta, from pretty much any provider, and either migrate, share or just move it from one place to the other. Perhaps ironically, this is also happening between AI agents. Tech connoisseurs find it easy to move from one model to another by simply migrating their context from one place to the other. The models themselves are not exempt from this. There was this belief for a while that everyone would just roll their own software and the cost of software would go to zero. I think that is very unlikely to happen. Public software won’t go to zero; the bar is just going to be much higher. Companies are unlikely to want to roll their own CRM or their own core banking system, simply because they want to focus on actually dealing with their customers, no matter how much AI capability they have. They want to use those AI capabilities to solve their customers’ issues, not necessarily to build a piece of infrastructure. What is true is that migrating away from these vendors has become a lot easier, and there should be less fear of doing it. The founder told me what he found when he went inside one client’s operation. “The complexity that exists as a part of their tech stack was kinda mind-blowing to me when I looked under the hood,” he said. “The fact that they still perform manual tasks to me is also quite surprising.” I would bet your own stack looks like that too, just smaller. So before the next renewal lands, price the exit. Ask a developer, or honestly just point a coding agent at it, and get a rough scope for moving your data and your integrations somewhere else. Then ask your vendor for a full export of your data in an open format, and watch what happens. And then negotiate a lot harder. You can review your vendors with a lot more certainty now, and you basically do not have to worry about your expenses so much, because none of them are locked in the way they used to be. The second direction is bigger, and it is the one I find more interesting: taking business away from big legacy companies. Every industry has its own version of the core providers — vendors that got comfortable because their clients could not realistically leave. “You’ve only got two or three providers that primarily power these institutions,” the founder said of his corner of the market, and “those core providers do not enable them to do what they want to do.”  Where some vendors have gotten lazy because they knew the client could not leave, you can now step in and give those clients what they actually need, and offer to handle the migration itself, the part that used to kill these deals. The pitch is the same exercise you just ran on your own vendors, pointed the other way: Show up with their exit already scoped. I actually ran this whole theory past him on the call: the idea that the locked-in vendors got lazy and that leaving is just not that hard anymore. “I think you’re spot on,” he said. You are not stuck anymore, so act like it, starting with whichever renewal hits your inbox next. Outcome pricing has been the norm in customer support for a year. The largest model vendor moving to it is a different matter. OpenAI logo OpenAI has begun letting some of its largest customers pay only when its AI actually completes the job. Kevin McLaughlin and Amir Efrati reported the change to The Information, giving the example of a customer support interaction handled end-to-end. The arrangement is limited to select major accounts rather than offered generally, and OpenAI has not announced it. TNW has not independently verified the report, and the terms, the customers, and the prices are all unknown. The industry name for this is outcome-based pricing, and the appeal to a finance director is not subtle. A bill that arrives only when something worked is considerably easier to defend than one that arrives regardless. Token billing has made that a live problem. One developer running a hundred agents in parallel accumulated $1.3m in OpenAI tokens across thirty days, which is an extreme case of a general pattern where cost scales with attempts rather than results. Customer support is where the model has already settled, because a resolution is one of the few AI outputs anyone can define. Intercom charges $0.99 for each conversation its Fin agent resolves, and nothing at all for the ones it does not. Zendesk went further in May, restricting billing to what it calls Verified Resolutions, confirmed by an LLM evaluation within 72 hours of the conversation. Assisted escalations and contained resolutions became free, and the billable rate sits at roughly $1.20 to $1.50 on committed volume. Salesforce has been working through the same question in public and more awkwardly. Agentforce launched at $2 per conversation, charged for every 24-hour session whether or not anything was resolved, which customers found both expensive and impossible to forecast. Flex Credits arrived as the answer, moving the meter from conversations to individual actions at about 10 cents each, starting at $500 for 100,000 credits. That is consumption pricing rather than outcome pricing, and the distinction matters, because an action that fails still bills. Buyers appear to want both, in that order. Futurum Group found in May that 43% of them prefer consumption-based models and 27% prefer outcome-based ones, with fewer than one in five still preferring to pay per user. “Outcome-based pricing is becoming a market standard,” wrote Keith Kirkpatrick, the firm’s research director for enterprise software, whose sharper finding is that vendors offering seats alone are now being disqualified before the evaluation starts. For OpenAI, the move is a change of position rather than a new product. It has sold capacity by the token, priced per model and per call, and letting an enterprise pay for completed work instead means accepting the risk that the work does not complete. That risk has to be priced somewhere, and the interesting question is where. A vendor confident in its success rate can afford the arrangement, while one that is not has to load the per-success price until the economics match, which is why per-resolution rates cluster around a dollar rather than a cent. It also changes who carries the cost of a bad answer. Under token billing, the customer pays for every failed attempt, whereas under outcome billing the vendor absorbs them, which is a meaningful transfer of risk from the buyer to the company that built the model. The harder part is agreeing what success means. A resolution is definable, but the agentic work OpenAI has been pushing towards, with 10 million users on its agents, involves multi-step tasks where completion is a matter of judgement rather than a field in a database. There is a commercial reason to want it settled quickly. An enterprise that cannot forecast a bill tends to run a pilot indefinitely rather than sign, and outcome pricing removes the objection at exactly the point in the sales cycle where it usually stalls. None of that is settled, and none of it is public. What is on the record is that the largest model vendor has started, quietly and selectively, to sell results instead of capacity. LUMI-AI goes to Kajaani in 2027, paid for by six countries and EuroHPC, and built by the company France bought from Atos in March. An architect’s visualisation of the LUMI-AI data centre in Kajaani, Finland. Europe is buying another AI supercomputer, and this one is headed to Kajaani in northern Finland. LUMI-AI is a €387.8 million system, roughly $449 million, that will be built by Bull, the French supercomputer maker that the French state bought outright five months ago. The order is the sixth AI Factory procurement contract signed by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, the body coordinating Europe’s publicly funded supercomputing infrastructure. The cost is being split evenly between EuroHPC and the LUMI AI Factory consortium, which is where the political logic behind the project becomes clearer. Finland, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Norway and Poland are all contributing to a machine that will sit on Finnish soil but be available to researchers and companies across the consortium. In practical terms, the new system is expected to deliver roughly ten times the AI capacity of the existing LUMI supercomputer, while nearly doubling its conventional high-performance computing capability. Deployment is scheduled for the second half of 2027, which may sound distant for an AI system, but is fairly standard for a major supercomputer procurement. The hardware is more revealing than the headline price. LUMI-AI will use AMD Instinct MI430X accelerators and sixth-generation EPYC processors with 256 cores, built around Bull’s BullSequana XH3500 architecture. There are two pieces of the system that give it a stronger European identity than simply assembling an American-designed machine on European soil. Bull is supplying its BXI interconnect, which links the nodes together, as well as its patented warm-water direct liquid cooling technology, both of which were developed in France. The wider supplier list also reflects an effort to keep more of the infrastructure within Europe. IBM Storage Scale will provide the storage layer, while Nokia is supplying the data centre networking, bringing a Finnish company into a system that will be installed in Finland. “LUMI-AI marks an important milestone for European AI and Bull’s leadership in energy-efficient, complex AI infrastructures,” said Emmanuel Le Roux, the company’s chief executive. Anders Jensen, who runs EuroHPC, presented the purchase as the sixth step in a broader sequence of AI infrastructure investments rather than an isolated project. Bull’s ownership makes the deal particularly significant. Atos completed the sale of its Advanced Computing business to the French state on 31 March, in a transaction with an enterprise value of up to €404 million, including €104 million in earn-outs, making the French government the company’s sole shareholder. The business generated around €700 million in revenue in 2025 and operates Europe’s only supercomputer manufacturing plant in Angers. It also builds the systems used to model France’s nuclear deterrent, giving the business a strategic importance that goes well beyond the commercial supercomputing market and helps explain why the French government was unwilling to see it disappear into foreign ownership. Kimmo Koski, who runs CSC, the Finnish research organisation that will host LUMI-AI, described the new system as a continuation of what the existing LUMI consortium has already built rather than a project starting from scratch. That existing track record is part of the reason six countries are prepared to pool funding around a facility located in a country that only one of them actually hosts. The arrangement fits a pattern that has been taking shape across Europe for the past two years. EuroHPC selected its first seven AI Factory sites in December 2024, followed by six more in October 2025, and procurement contracts have been signed progressively since then. The gigafactories were supposed to take that effort to another scale, with a €30 billion programme covering seven much larger sites. Progress on that part of the strategy has been slower, however. The gigafactory programme has been struggling with delays that have frustrated some of the partners it needs, while the projects themselves are considerably more complicated than building an individual supercomputer at an established site. Even the AI Factories that are now being procured remain relatively small compared with what the biggest private technology companies are building. A €387.8 million supercomputer represents only a fraction of the investment behind a single hyperscaler campus, so Europe’s response to that imbalance has so far relied heavily on pooling resources between governments rather than trying to match the private sector project for project. Kajaani also has an advantage that many potential European sites cannot easily reproduce. Finland has abundant relatively cheap, low-carbon electricity and a climate that makes cooling large computing installations considerably easier, and the country has spent years developing the infrastructure needed to turn those conditions into a competitive advantage for data centres and supercomputing. With Germany’s Jupiter now joining the European supercomputing landscape, LUMI remains one of the continent’s most established large-scale systems. The decision to buy from a state-owned supplier is perhaps the clearest indication of how much the European approach has changed. Three years ago, government ownership of a major supercomputer manufacturer would have been an unusual detail in a procurement story. Now France owns the vendor, six governments are helping finance the machine, and the accelerators at its core are still made by an American company.
